sources.channel: Top Tennis Training - Pro Tennis Lessons

good_form: In the unit turn, keep the right elbow bent at about 90 degrees, as Djokovic, Alcaraz and Nadal do.
Let the racket drop fluidly into the backswing so it sits on the hitting side of the body, rather than lifting the arm up and back.
Start the acceleration from the ground up: leg drive and rotation as a kinetic chain, using the big muscles. Footwork such as the transfer move, lateral hop or front-foot hop helps.

Accelerate by pulling the arm away from the body, travelling from the right hip away from the trunk. Alcaraz's arm travels down and away, Federer's and Nadal's travels up and away. This counter force creates the racket flip and topspin.
At contact, keep the arm in front of the body with the wrist extended, palm facing the net and racket pointing toward the side fence.
Keep the wrist loose and relaxed through acceleration and contact, powering the swing with the pec, shoulder and whole kinetic chain.

faults.name: Straight arm in unit turn
faults.looks_like: The arm is straight, not bent at 90 degrees, during the unit turn.
faults.why_it_matters: Makes the forehand feel tight, rushed or late, and stops the racket dropping smoothly into the backswing.
causes: Taking the racket back with too much right-arm energy
fixes: Check that the right elbow is bent at 90 degrees in the unit turn, so the racket can drop fluidly and accelerate with ease
Film your stroke and compare it with the top players
outcome_effects: Tight, rushed or late forehand
Loss of effortless acceleration

faults.name: Taking the arm up and back in the backswing
faults.looks_like: Instead of dropping, the arm lifts up and then goes back into the backswing position.
faults.why_it_matters: It costs fluid momentum and the racket flip position.
causes: Not trusting a simple fluid drop of the arm
fixes: Set the arm down fluidly with the bent-elbow unit turn, then use the natural acceleration to go forward and up
Aim for the racket on the hitting side of the body, away from it
outcome_effects: Less fluid momentum
No clean racket flip position

faults.name: Arm-only acceleration without the legs
faults.looks_like: The player just steps and swings, with most of the power generated from the arm instead of the legs driving and rotating.
faults.why_it_matters: The kinetic chain is not used, so power and spin are limited. The speaker says this is especially common in older players.
causes: Not starting the swing from the ground up
Not focusing on footwork or leg force
fixes: Consciously focus on the force generated from the legs
Use footwork such as the transfer move, lateral hop or front-foot hop
outcome_effects: Less power and spin

faults.name: Arm bending in toward the body on acceleration
faults.looks_like: The arm bends and travels toward the center of the body instead of away from it.
faults.why_it_matters: It prevents the racket flip and the heavy topspin.
causes: Not having the proper backswing position
fixes: Achieve the key backswing position
Pull the arm away from the body, from the right hip away from the trunk, with the Alcaraz down-and-away or Federer/Nadal up-and-away path
outcome_effects: No racket flip
Less topspin

faults.name: Wrist flexion at contact
faults.looks_like: The wrist is flexed at contact and in the follow-through, and the arm is too close to the body.
faults.why_it_matters: It leads to wrist pain, tension, lost consistency and frustration, and the swing feels tight and weak. The speaker calls it the number one mistake. Pain and tension are mentioned as results, but the speaker doesn't explicitly warn of injury risk, so this is marked as form.
causes: Trying to generate power from the wrist
Contact with the arm from shoulder to elbow too close to the body
Tight wrist instead of relaxed
fixes: Make contact with the arm in front of the body and the wrist extended, palm toward the net
Drill 1: shadow swings stopping at the contact position, then fed balls stopping at contact, then build up to full power
Keep the wrist deliberately loose through contact, powering with the pec, shoulder and kinetic chain
Drill 2: grip the racket with only the index and middle fingers and shadow swing with a relaxed wrist, for a deeper racket flip and more stretch-shortening, then apply it to fed balls
outcome_effects: Ball sails long
Loss of consistency
Feels tight and weak
Less topspin

good_form: Unit turn starts right after the split step, once you read the ball coming to the forehand, with a smooth rotation of the core.
At the end of the unit turn, the left hand is on the throat (choke) of the racket and you can see the racket through your eyes from behind.
At the end of the unit turn the right elbow is roughly in line with the shoulders, perhaps slightly to one side, and the strings point at the side fence.
Backswing is fluid and uses two right-arm motions: slight abduction with the elbow going back, then elbow extension; the left arm straightens out.

At the end of the backswing the arm to the elbow is in line with the shoulders, the racket tip is up at about 45 degrees and the strings angle down, so the racket stays closed on acceleration and gives easy power from the shoulder.
Acceleration comes in two parts: legs drive first, then trunk rotates while the arm moves.
The arm does shoulder flexion (upward), horizontal shoulder adduction (up and forward) and external rotation of the shoulder to create the flip; wrist extension follows passively.
The racket travels an arc, going away from the body then toward it; the midpoint is the transition point, where a straight path becomes a rotational path and topspin is generated.
At contact, bent or straight arm is much the same: the shoulder-to-elbow segment points in front of the body at about 45 degrees toward the net post.
At contact the wrist is in an extended position, and the elbow angle stays at 160 degrees or less bent than straight (not past 160 as described).

In the follow-through, the upper arm segment from shoulder to elbow keeps extending forward and out through the ball; follow-throughs vary on tour (Nadal buggy whip, feather extension, Djokovic spin).
The wrist produces a topspin windshield-wiper motion in the follow-through.

faults.name: Taking the racket back with just the arm
faults.looks_like: On the unit turn the racket is moved back by the arm alone instead of by body rotation.
faults.why_it_matters: It creates tension in the right arm and makes it harder to rotate with the whole body.
fixes: Rotate the core smoothly so the whole body takes the racket back.
outcome_effects: Tension in the right arm
Harder to rotate the whole body

faults.name: Right arm too straight in unit turn
faults.looks_like: The right arm is too straight as the unit turn begins.
faults.why_it_matters: It adds complexity and unnecessary motion to the backswing position.
fixes: Get the right elbow roughly in line with the shoulders with the strings toward the side fence.
outcome_effects: Extra unnecessary motion in the backswing

faults.name: Arm too far back with open racket face
faults.looks_like: Out of the unit turn the arm travels too far back with the racket face open.
faults.why_it_matters: It misses the correct backswing checkpoint of a closed racket.
fixes: Finish with the arm to the elbow in line with the shoulders, tip up at about 45 degrees and strings angled down.
outcome_effects: Racket not kept closed on acceleration, losing easy power from the shoulder

faults.name: Pre-flipped racket tip
faults.looks_like: The arm is in the right spot but the racket tip is at about 90 to 100 degrees relative to the net instead of up and away at about 45 degrees.
faults.why_it_matters: It gives up the closed racket and easy shoulder power of the correct backswing.
fixes: Keep the tip up and away at about 45 degrees with the strings angled down.
outcome_effects: Racket not kept closed on acceleration

faults.name: Accelerating down and in
faults.looks_like: The arm travels down and in by flexing the bicep and wrist instead of going up and away.
faults.why_it_matters: It goes against the up-and-away arc path the acceleration needs.
fixes: Accelerate on an up and away path using shoulder flexion, horizontal adduction and external rotation.

faults.name: Stroke started by the arm instead of the legs
faults.looks_like: The stroke is initiated from the arm rather than the leg drive.
faults.why_it_matters: The acceleration should be a two-part process with legs first and then trunk rotation.
fixes: Drive with the legs first, then rotate the trunk, then let the arm move.

faults.name: Arm too bent at contact
faults.looks_like: The elbow angle at contact is past 160 degrees of bend, i.e. the arm is too bent.
faults.why_it_matters: It produces a biomechanical position with less power and less topspin.
fixes: Keep at least about 160 degrees of elbow angle at contact, as Djokovic does with a bent arm.
outcome_effects: Less power
Less topspin

faults.name: Arm too close to trunk or abducted at contact
faults.looks_like: At contact the arm is too close to the trunk or in a more abducted position, with the wrist compensating by flexing.
faults.why_it_matters: It weakens contact and causes tension and weakness in the wrist.
causes: Wrong arm position relative to the body at contact
fixes: Put the arm in front of the body with shoulder-to-elbow about 45 degrees in front of the torso, and the wrist extended.
outcome_effects: Weakened contact
Wrist flexed and tense

faults.name: Arm stops and bends across the body in follow-through
faults.looks_like: Instead of extending forward and out, the arm stops accelerating and bends in across the body.
faults.why_it_matters: You feel like you hit hard but get no effortless pop.
fixes: Keep the shoulder-to-elbow segment extending forward and out through the ball.
outcome_effects: No effortless pop

faults.name: Wrist flexing in at contact instead of windshield wiper
faults.looks_like: The wrist flexes in at contact rather than producing a topspin windshield-wiper motion.
faults.why_it_matters: It creates tension, weakness and lost consistency, and prevents a confident forehand pop.
fixes: Let the wrist make a topspin windshield-wiper motion.
outcome_effects: Tension and weakness
Lost consistency
Less pop

good_form: Make contact with the ball out in front of the body, ideally in front of the shoes, because that is the most stable and strong position.
Contact height is generally between waist and shoulder; heavy topspin grips (semi-western/western) prefer slightly higher, eastern/continental prefer lower.
Use the ready, read, react checklist: be prepared with a split step, read the ball's height, speed, depth and spin, then move and prepare racket and feet early.
Use the non-dominant hand to take the racket back with a unit turn so the whole body turns rather than just the hitting arm.
The non-dominant hand helps balance and centre of gravity, engages more muscle groups, and can help drive the racket through by pulling the elbow back.
Choose take-back size to suit the need: bigger for power against slower balls, smaller for timing and control against fast balls.
A somewhat smaller take-back usually gives much more control while the shot stays surprisingly powerful.

faults.name: Wrong positioning / late contact point
faults.looks_like: Meeting the ball when it is beside or behind the body, being too close (cramped) or too far away, and then forcing the ball back into play with the wrist.
faults.why_it_matters: Contact out in front gives the most control of the racket head, strength and stability; late contact loses this.
causes: Not being ready for the ball (no split step, poor court position)
Misreading the ball's height, speed, depth or spin (the most common breakdown)
Reacting too slowly, with late racket or foot preparation
fixes: Go through the ready-read-react checklist to find where it breaks down
Hit more balls and play more matches against varied styles and paces to improve reading
Two-touch tennis: tap the ball up softly, let it bounce, adjust position, then hit over the net
One-legged tennis: set up and hit on one leg and hold balance; being too far or too close makes you lose balance
Practise with a double-handed forehand, which forces a better position since you can't afford to be far from the ball
outcome_effects: Wrist is used to force the ball back into play
Loss of balance when too far or too close
Less control and less strength through the shot

faults.name: Not using the non-dominant hand
faults.looks_like: Taking the racket back with only the hitting arm while the non-dominant hand dangles at the side or splits away, with no unit turn.
faults.why_it_matters: The hitting arm has to do much more work, which can lead to injuries and reduced control, and it loses efficient power.
causes: Hitting with just the dominant arm instead of turning the whole body
Trying to hit the ball hard, which makes mistakes creep in
fixes: Self feeds: from ready position hold a ball in the spare hand, turn sideways, drop the ball and hit in front of the body
Catch-drop-hit: catch an oncoming ball with the non-dominant hand, then drop and hit from the same position
Double-handed forehand to force the upper body turn and bringing the spare hand with you
Imagine handcuffs: hands stay close on the way back until the ball bounces, then separate and use the spare arm to come back
Use the left (non-dominant) hand to take the racket back and pull the elbow back to help drive the racket through
outcome_effects: Racket is less likely to go in play
Less control
Power has to be forced rather than coming from torso, hips and shoulders

faults.name: Take-back too big
faults.looks_like: A large backswing that takes a long path.
faults.why_it_matters: A big take-back takes more time, so contact is late and hard to get in front; a smaller swing makes timing easier and gives more control and consistency.
causes: Not being aware of how big your swing really is
Taking a big swing against fast incoming balls with too little time
Trying for power
fixes: Video your forehand to see the real take-back size, then practise and video again
Exaggerate a tiny take-back to find a middle ground
Practise against lower or faster balls from a partner, machine or coach to limit the time available
Stand sideways with the non-dominant side to a fence or wall so a too-big take-back hits it
Stand with your back to the fence or wall for a very compact swing, such as return of serve
outcome_effects: Catching the ball late
Contact point not in front
Less control and consistency

good_form: In defense and rally phases, hit crosscourt; save down the line for attack or finish phases.
Crosscourt gives more court length on the diagonal, goes over the lower middle of the net, pulls the opponent farther out, and needs less recovery.
Prepare coiled: hips and chest sideways, off-hand arm across the body.
Legs drive the back hip through before the racket comes through.
As the hips start to move, drive the off-hand elbow back and tuck the arm toward the chest to speed rotation and racket head speed.
Hold the closed position as long as possible and don't open up early before driving into the ball.
For a driving, arced forehand from the back of the court, finish with the elbow slightly above the contact point to accelerate up the back of the ball.
Use a short backswing and a long follow-through for better timing, hitting zone, directional control and depth.
Pair the short backswing with coiling and leg drive to regain power.
Grip loosely so the elbow and wrist move naturally and release the energy built from the legs and torso, allowing the hand to roll over the ball for topspin.
Keep body weight moving forward, or at least neutral, into the ball.
Position yourself farther back against heavy hitters to have room to step in; read the depth of the incoming ball early.
When hit at your feet, widen the base for stability and to hold your ground rather than lean back.

faults.name: Wrong shot for the phase of play
faults.looks_like: Going down the line when in defense or rally mode, or choosing risky shots on the favored forehand side.
faults.why_it_matters: It is where most unforced errors come from and can give the opponent an easy passing shot.
causes: Favoring the forehand tempts players into higher risk shots
Too many options and poor decisions about the phase of play
fixes: Stick to crosscourt as much as possible in defense and rally
Save down the line for attack and finish phases
Trust that the opponent will rush and go down the line first, making errors or offering a safer crosscourt winner
outcome_effects: Unforced errors
Easy passing shot for the opponent

faults.name: Splitting the hands too early
faults.looks_like: Pulling the off hand away and opening the chest to the court before hitting the ball.
faults.why_it_matters: Off hand is vital for efficiency, balance and control; opening early loses directional control.
causes: Preparing well but pulling the off hand away before contact
fixes: Stay coiled with hips and chest sideways and the arm across the body
Drive the off-hand elbow back and tuck it to the chest as the hips start moving
Hold the position as long as possible until ready to drive into the ball
outcome_effects: Ball sprays
Dragging the ball across to the left
Catching the ball late and hitting it to the right
Less rotation speed, depth and spin

faults.name: Backswing too big, follow-through too short
faults.looks_like: A large backswing followed by stopping the swing quickly after contact.
faults.why_it_matters: The big backswing takes longer and causes late contact, costing consistency and power; working only on the follow-through doesn't fix the root problem.
causes: Unnecessarily big backswing
Catching the ball late, then trying to control the ball by stopping quickly
fixes: Shorten the backswing and lengthen the follow-through
Combine with coiling and leg drive to regain power
Accept an initial loss of power in exchange for control
outcome_effects: Inconsistency
Lack of power
Poor timing
Reduced hitting zone, directional control and depth

faults.name: Gripping the racket too tightly
faults.looks_like: Tight grip tensing the forearm muscles so the racket moves in one plane, swiping across the body instead of rolling over the ball.
faults.why_it_matters: It limits the elbow and wrist range, blocks the release of energy from legs and torso, and reduces shoulder internal rotation.
causes: Worn overgrip makes you grip hard to avoid dropping the racket
Tension in the arm
fixes: Replace the overgrip often
Breathe out as you hit to loosen the arm and tense the core
outcome_effects: Less power
Shorter hitting zone
Not going all the way through the ball
Swipe across the body, no heavy topspin roll

faults.name: Losing the collision with the ball
faults.looks_like: Being pushed onto the back foot with body weight traveling backwards.
faults.why_it_matters: Body weight should travel forward or stay neutral, not backward.
causes: Standing too close against a heavy or deep ball
Poor reading of the ball's depth
Good shot hit at your feet
fixes: Stand farther back against big hitters to have room to step in
Read depth early and get back far enough to move forward
Widen the base against balls at the feet for stability and to stay neutral
outcome_effects: Leaning back
Reduced stability and control

good_form: Think of two forces and two planes: backwards-to-forwards (horizontal) and down-to-up (vertical); down-to-up is only half the picture.
At contact keep the racket face slightly tilted forward, not vertical.
Imagine hitting up an incline, like a steep slope or mountain, rather than up a vertical wall.
The incline of the swing is what sends the ball over the net.
The forward-tilted face grips the ball and, moving upward, creates forward rotation (topspin) so the ball drops into the court.
Keep the racket face stable and the strings facing forward/down after contact, as Alcaraz and Zverev do, rather than facing the sky.
Practice in order: forward-angled racket face first, then the forward slope/mountain swing cue.

faults.name: Hitting purely down to up with a vertical racket face
faults.looks_like: Racket face is straight up and down at contact, and after contact the strings point up toward the sky.
faults.why_it_matters: It leads to shanks, balls dumped in the net, and little or no topspin, so the ball pops up.
causes: Thinking only about the vertical down-to-up plane and ignoring the backwards-to-forwards plane
Focusing too much on going down to up, possibly because they were taught that way
Imagining hitting up a vertical wall
fixes: Keep a slightly forward-tilted racket face at contact
Imagine hitting up a steep slope or mountain instead of a wall
Drills: shadow strokes, topspin-checking device, ball on racket bag at an incline and brush up, ball drops, live balls crosscourt then down the line
outcome_effects: Shanked balls off the frame or inside of the racket
Ball spills into the net with no power
Ball pops up with little or no topspin
Rolling over the ball makes it go into the net

good_form: Rotation is the most important technical element of the forehand; it is a big power source and also determines contact point and swing path.
Rotation has always been part of the forehand, not just the modern one: the upper body starts pointing one way and finishes pointing the opposite way.
Judge contact by shoulder position: the dominant shoulder should be in front of the non-dominant shoulder at contact.
Start the rotation slightly before the racket goes forward.
Use the loop: as the racket loops up and drops, it is easier to sequence the rotation; begin opening up toward the bottom of the racket drop.
On the run, ideally hit off the non-dominant foot dynamically, rotating while one foot is in the air so the torso is freed up.
If there is time on a wide ball, set the outside foot to break the momentum carrying you sideways, which makes rotation more natural.
When running around the backhand, set the feet late in the stroke, around the racket drop, so the leftward movement helps the right-to-left rotation.
When pushed back, keep the body behind the ball and hit off the back (dominant) foot, letting the non-dominant foot swing backward so the body rotates freely.
When pushed back, having the back foot slightly on the outside makes rotation more intuitive; closed feet are fine if you hit off the back foot with the other foot in the air.

On a short forehand, turn toward the forehand side as soon as you see the ball is coming to that side, but only a three-quarter turn with the chest pointing slightly into the court so you can still run forward.

faults.name: Not opening up early enough
faults.looks_like: The player rotates but the timing is late, so the dominant shoulder is behind at contact.
faults.why_it_matters: Contact ends up late and behind; it is a common trap at lower recreational levels.
causes: Rotation is not sequenced correctly; it does not begin before the racket goes forward.
fixes: Initiate rotation slightly before the racket moves forward.
Use the loop and start opening up toward the bottom of the racket drop.
outcome_effects: Contact is made with the dominant shoulder behind.

faults.name: Lateral momentum to the right on a running forehand
faults.looks_like: Moving sideways toward the forehand side, the player doesn't rotate enough or at all, contacting with the dominant shoulder far back.
faults.why_it_matters: Body momentum goes opposite to the right-to-left rotation, locking the torso.
causes: Body weight naturally travels toward the right while rotation goes right to left.
Feet are planted while momentum carries sideways, locking the torso.
fixes: Hit a dynamic shot off the non-dominant foot, rotating while one foot is in midair.
If there is time, set the outside foot to break the momentum.
outcome_effects: Contact with the dominant shoulder far behind.

faults.name: Running around the backhand without setting the feet
faults.looks_like: Moving backward and leftward without planting the feet, the right side can't rotate forward.
faults.why_it_matters: Rotation becomes nearly impossible and the player is left in trouble.
causes: Moving backwards without setting the feet, so momentum carries the player to the left during the stroke.
fixes: Set the feet, ideally late in the stroke around the racket drop, so the leftward movement helps the right-to-left rotation.
outcome_effects: Contact is way behind the body.
Weak shot.
Whole open side of the court is exposed.

faults.name: Letting the ball get behind the body
faults.looks_like: Contact is made back behind the body when pushed back in the court.
faults.why_it_matters: It is impossible to rotate when contacting back there.
causes: Being pushed back and not moving the feet fast enough.
fixes: Be quick with footwork and keep the body behind the ball.
Hit off the back foot and let the non-dominant foot swing backward so the body rotates freely.
Keep the back foot slightly on the outside.
outcome_effects: You can only moonball the ball back.
Hitting hard from there sprays the ball wildly.

faults.name: Running straight at a short ball without turning
faults.looks_like: Running straight up to a short forehand without turning the body.
faults.why_it_matters: Contact is in front but there is zero rotation.
causes: Not turning to the forehand side when recognizing the ball is coming there.
fixes: Turn as soon as you recognize a forehand, using a three-quarter turn with the chest pointing slightly into the court, not a full turn.
outcome_effects: Zero rotation on the shot.

good_form: Begin the take back as soon as the ball leaves the machine or the opponent's racket, without waiting for the bounce.
The take back is mainly turning the body, with the racket going along for the ride.
Keep the racket up on the way back, then let it drop once behind you and circle forward in a C-shaped swing so it never has to stop.
Close the racket face below contact, with the strings tilted down, then swing up the back of the ball to create topspin.
Keep turning right away and keep the racket up as you turn, while also closing the face for spin.
Use the non-hitting hand in three ways: help the racket back to coil, hold it up so it is visible over the non-hitting shoulder at contact, and catch the racket at the finish.
Turn with both hands, then hold the catch for a second at the end.
Pick a specific air target over the net on every forehand, aiming for it 100% of the time even if you miss.
The farther back you stand, the higher you aim over the net. The farther forward in the court, the lower you aim.
Vary net clearance: low (within about a foot) to hit hard or give a low volley, medium (three to four feet) for depth, and high for lobs or high balls to the backhand.

faults.name: Waiting for the bounce before taking the racket back
faults.looks_like: The player waits until the ball bounces, then pulls the racket back, so the racket is still out in front when the ball arrives.
faults.why_it_matters: It makes the player late all the time, and it is one reason players struggle to take the ball on the rise.
causes: Not starting the take back until the ball has bounced
fixes: Begin the take back as soon as you see the ball come off the machine or the opponent's racket.
Make the take back a body turn and let the racket go along with it.
outcome_effects: Late contact, especially against balls with a lot of spin, depth or speed
Trouble hitting on-the-rise balls that land deep and are hit right after the bounce

faults.name: Taking the racket down twice
faults.looks_like: The racket goes down on the way back and then drops down again before swinging forward (down, down).
faults.why_it_matters: The racket has to stop in order to come back forward, so you struggle against hard hitters.
causes: Dropping the racket on the way back, before the normal drop behind the body
fixes: Keep the racket up on the way back and let it drop only once, behind you.
Swing in a C shape or circle so the racket keeps moving without slowing.
outcome_effects: Racket stops and cannot flow forward smoothly
Struggling against really hard hitters

faults.name: Hitting every ball flat
faults.looks_like: The racket is straight up and down in the back, so the swing goes flat into the ball.
faults.why_it_matters: Flat hitting is not necessarily wrong, but it is limiting and gives you no variety, such as dipping the ball at feet, topspin lobs, or safe height over the net.
causes: Racket held straight up and down in the back instead of closed below contact
fixes: Practice closing the racket face, with the strings tilted down, and spinning up the back of the ball.
Keep turning right away and keep the racket up while you close the face.
Swing up with confidence, since more upward swing with a closed face gives more spin.
outcome_effects: Can't dip the ball at an opponent's feet as they come forward
Can't hit a topspin lob
Can't get height that safely comes down before the baseline

faults.name: Misusing the non-hitting hand
faults.looks_like: The non-hitting arm dangles at the side, or points at the ball and then hugs the body as if in a straight jacket. The hand is not visible over the non-hitting shoulder at contact, and the racket is not caught at the finish.
faults.why_it_matters: The non-hitting hand should help coil and uncoil and clear the way for the hips. Most recreational players do not use it correctly.
causes: Letting the non-hitting arm hang down at the side
Pointing at the ball with the non-hitting hand, which leads to hugging yourself
fixes: Turn with both hands.
At contact, have the non-hitting hand visible over the non-hitting shoulder.
Catch the racket in the non-hitting hand at the finish and hold it for a second.
Check on video that the hand was up when you hit; catching the racket helps confirm this.
outcome_effects: Hips can't turn when you point and hug yourself
The racket can't come through freely

faults.name: Not picking an air target over the net
faults.looks_like: Hitting forehands without a specific target height over the net in mind.
faults.why_it_matters: You should aim at an air target 100% of the time, even if you do not always hit it, as a basketball shooter aims at the hoop on every shot.
causes: No specific target over the net chosen before the shot
fixes: Pick an air target on every shot, aiming higher the farther back you are and lower the farther forward you are.
Vary the target height between low, medium and high depending on the shot you want.
outcome_effects: Less control over depth and net clearance

good_form: Start the swing early enough to make contact out in front of the body.
Set the body up in the right position before swinging so efficient biomechanics can be used, e.g. stepping in for neutral or moving out for open stance.
Make a good unit turn with the back or outside leg loaded by the time you arrive at the ball.
On a wide forehand, use split step, drop step and unit turn while moving so you are loaded on arrival.
Stay far enough from the ball; for a waist-height neutral stance forehand, the strings should meet the ball at waist height with more room than arm's length.
Stand a little closer for low balls and further away for higher balls, especially shoulder-height balls.
Time the hip drive relative to the ball's bounce: as a starting point begin as it bounces, earlier for low hard flat balls, just after the bounce for high floating balls.
Sequence the kinetic chain hip, then torso, then arm, adjusting speed and swing path to each shot.
A simplified option is a unit turn, racket set in a position, then swing through to contact with hip drive and the wrist lagged, skipping the extra steps of the pro (ATP) swing.

faults.name: Late or poor preparation
faults.looks_like: Starting the swing too late and not getting the body into the right set-up position (unit turn, back leg loaded), especially on harder balls or in matches.
faults.why_it_matters: Without quick, correct preparation you can't get contact out in front or use efficient biomechanics, and timing can never be fixed.
causes: Habit not built, so it breaks down in match situations
Visual system not reading the ball's flight quickly, esp. short, deep or variable balls
Having habituated slow movement and slow footwork
fixes: Focus on preparation in practice with many repetitions until it is habit
Train the visual system (brain-based training class)
Practice footwork patterns over and over to move faster (short forehand, wide forehand)
Record yourself in both practice and points to see if it is your issue
outcome_effects: Contact not out in front
Cannot use efficient biomechanics
Preparation falls apart on difficult shots and in matches

faults.name: Standing too close to the ball
faults.looks_like: Setting up about arm's length or less from the ball, then compensating by bending the arm, over-rotating, pulling off the shot, snatching at it or bending the wrist.
faults.why_it_matters: It makes the shot nearly impossible to hit with efficient biomechanics, particularly on shoulder-height balls.
causes: Poor spacing habits
Late preparation because the ball isn't read quickly or accurately
Lack of practiced tennis footwork patterns, especially for those who didn't grow up playing
fixes: Practice staying further from the ball on each feed type: neutral, open stance, short, high
Train the visual system
Practice footwork patterns off court (split step, drop step, unit turn on the move) until habitual; free footwork program mentioned
outcome_effects: Bent arm, over-rotation, pulling off or snatching the shot, wrist bending
Inefficient biomechanics

faults.name: Poor timing of the swing
faults.looks_like: Starting the swing and hip drive at the wrong moment relative to the ball's flight and bounce, and trying to use the arm too much.
faults.why_it_matters: Each shot reacts differently off the court (low flat, high topspin, slice), so the swing start and kinetic chain sequence must be adjusted; timing is hard and a common struggle.
causes: Underlying preparation problems
Visual system not good enough to read speed, distance and bounce
Insufficient coordination to adjust swing speed, path and sequencing
Trying to use advanced pro technique beyond current skill level
fixes: Work with a ball machine on one specific feed at a time, a few hundred reps each, before changing feed
Time hip drive to the bounce: start at the bounce as a baseline, before it for low hard flat balls, just after for high floating balls
Build a memory bank of what timing fits what ball
Train vision and coordination with brain-based training
Simplify the swing to a unit turn, racket set, then swing through while still driving hip, torso, arm
outcome_effects: Inconsistent tennis, with occasional great shots but many misses
Contact not out in front on low hard balls if hips start too late
Starting too soon on high floating balls

faults.name: Copying the pro's complex forehand technique too early
faults.looks_like: Trying the ATP forehand: unit turn, hip drive at the right time, racket lag with butt cap pointing at the ball, then flipping the racket over.
faults.why_it_matters: It is the best way to hit if you have the skill, but without it timing is hard and results are inconsistent.
causes: Coaches and videos telling players to imitate pros
fixes: Simplify: unit turn, racket into a set position, then swing through to contact
Keep hip, torso, arm drive and lagged wrist but with fewer movement steps
outcome_effects: Inconsistent forehand with many missed shots

good_form: Keep the non-dominant hand from travelling past the middle of the body during the unit turn; stop there and separate it from the hitting hand.
Stopping the turn at the middle lets you come out of it and make contact with the dominant shoulder in front.
Bent arm or straight arm forehand both work; which one you use is down to genetic predisposition, so play with the arm style that comes naturally.
Wrist lag is present on every forehand and should happen naturally, as a product of torso rotation and stroke acceleration.
Most ATP players swing on a vertical path at contact, with the racket tip pointing to the side and going up over the ball.
The wrist is passive at contact, even for Nadal; it only becomes active around shoulder height after contact.
Think about finishing the stroke strongly across the body, and the wrist will end up in place naturally.

faults.name: Turn too large
faults.looks_like: The non-dominant hand stays on the racket and travels past the middle of the body toward the back shoulder during the unit turn.
faults.why_it_matters: Recreational players usually cannot unwind from such a big turn, whereas pros can still sync the stroke and make contact with the dominant shoulder in front.
causes: Copying the extra-large turn of pros like Djokovic
fixes: Do not let the non-dominant hand go past the middle of the body.
Release the non-hitting hand from the racket at the middle of the body.
Use the lace line as a reference for the middle of the body.
outcome_effects: Contact is made with the dominant shoulder behind.

faults.name: Forcing a straight arm
faults.looks_like: A bent-arm player tries to straighten the arm during preparation as Nadal and Federer do.
faults.why_it_matters: The effort is pointless because the arm returns to a bend anyway, and contact is over in milliseconds so you cannot feel whether the arm is bent or straight.
causes: Copying the straight-arm forehand of Nadal and Federer
Not realizing that arm style depends on genetic predisposition
fixes: If you naturally hit with a bent arm, do not try to straighten it.
Accept that bent or straight does not matter.
outcome_effects: The arm goes back into a bend at contact anyway.

faults.name: Fake wrist lag
faults.looks_like: The player freezes the racket in the lag position, then consciously flips the racket back going forward, producing a hitch in the stroke.
faults.why_it_matters: It slows the stroke down in a crucial phase and is easy to spot.
causes: Consciously trying to create the wrist lag seen in high-level players
Not realizing the lag is a result of torso rotation and acceleration
fixes: Do not think about wrist lag at all.
Let it happen naturally by rotating the torso and accelerating the stroke correctly.
outcome_effects: The stroke slows and looks hitchy.

faults.name: Actively rolling the wrist at contact
faults.looks_like: An isolated wrist flick or roll over the ball at contact, with the stroke shortened and ending early.
faults.why_it_matters: The wrist is a small fragile part of the body and cannot generate much power; pros keep it passive at contact.
causes: Interpreting the vertical swing path as a wrist movement
Consciously thinking about using the wrist at contact, which slows the stroke before contact
fixes: Do not think about the wrist at all.
Think about finishing strongly across the body so the wrist falls into place.
outcome_effects: Loss of power
Loss of control, spraying the ball
Framing the ball or hitting the frame edges
Abruptly shortened stroke

good_form: Grip is the static rotation angle of the racket in your hand; if it's wrong, your contact angle will be wrong even if everything else is right.
Check the grip by where the tip of the middle and ring fingers sit on the eight-sided handle: for topspin forehand, on a short side followed by an open medium side.
Medium sides of the handle line up with the racket's edge; long sides line up with the racket's face. Also use the right grip size.
Put the non-hitting hand on the racket neck for the ready position, feet spaced wide, in a slight isometric squat.
The forehand ready position has the racket mostly horizontal; there are five distinct ready positions in tennis.
Turn the body to the right and push the arm back using deltoid and triceps; don't loop the arm, even though the racket head appears to loop.
At the end of preparation the racket faces back like a stop sign, pointing up with strings facing back or angled slightly down.
Take a full preparation when you have time; shorten it only when the ball is coming fast.
Stay in open stance rather than stepping into every ball, so you save time, energy and space.
Use open stance to do space correction: swing and gallop toward the ball if too far, or away from it if too close.
Swing by pulling the arm down with the lats, rotating the shoulder open, then pulling up to contact about northeast of the body.
Beginners or those without much strength should use an open contact angle; strong players can hit with a closed angle. Change contact angle with the shoulder, not the wrist.
After contact, bend the wrist in, turn the forearm around, close the chest and bend the elbow (chest and biceps), with the front deltoid pulling upward.
Finish around the tricep, deltoid, or over the trap, depending on height; a higher finish sends the ball higher and a lower finish sends it lower.
Legs are complementary, not the main power source; the arm leads, but legs shouldn't be locked.
Sequence the legs: slight isometric squat in ready position, slight right-side lunge during the take-back, then a slight calf raise during the swing, synchronized with the arm.

faults.name: Wrong grip
faults.looks_like: Middle and ring fingertips are not on a short side followed by an open medium side aligned with the racket edge.
faults.why_it_matters: The grip sets the contact angle, so a wrong grip makes you miss the stroke even if everything else is correct.
causes: Wrong rotation angle of the racket in the hand
fixes: Place the middle and ring fingertips on a short side followed by an open medium side aligned with the racket edge
Check the grip size fits your hand
outcome_effects: Contact angle is wrong and the ball is missed

faults.name: Night-sword (vertical center) ready position
faults.looks_like: Holding the racket vertically in the center in front of the body.
faults.why_it_matters: The ready position should equip you for the stroke you're about to hit; this one prepares you for nothing.
fixes: Hold the racket mostly horizontal in a forehand ready position with the non-hitting hand on the neck, feet apart, in a slight isometric squat

faults.name: Stepping into closed stance on every ball
faults.looks_like: Turning sideways and stepping into the court toward the ball.
faults.why_it_matters: It costs time, energy and space, and prevents space correction footwork.
causes: Coaches telling you to step into every ball
fixes: Stay in open stance and shift weight into the ball
Use swing and gallop to fix the distance
outcome_effects: Too close to the ball: the forehand gets cramped (T-Rex arm)
Too far from the ball: you bend over and break your back

faults.name: Looping the arm on take-back
faults.looks_like: Making a loop with the arm while taking the racket back.
faults.why_it_matters: The arm should push back, not loop; the racket only appears to loop.
causes: Inferring arm action by watching the racket instead of the arm
fixes: Turn the body and push the arm back with deltoid and triceps
Then pull down and swing up

faults.name: Brushing up with a closed angle when lacking strength
faults.looks_like: Brushing up on the ball with a closed contact angle when not hitting hard.
faults.why_it_matters: Brushing up only works when hitting hard.
causes: Not having much strength yet (beginner)
fixes: Use an open contact angle, adjusting it with the shoulder, not the wrist
outcome_effects: Ball goes straight into the net

faults.name: Finishing below the elbow
faults.looks_like: Swinging through and ending the forehand lower than the elbow.
faults.why_it_matters: The speaker calls it a critical error.
fixes: Finish around the tricep, deltoid or over the trap depending on your height
outcome_effects: A lower finish sends the ball lower

faults.name: Relying on legs for power / locked legs
faults.looks_like: Driving with the legs while the arm is still, or keeping the legs locked.
faults.why_it_matters: The legs are complementary and the arm leads; locked joints are undesirable.
causes: Belief that most power comes from the legs
fixes: Let the arm lead and use squat, right lunge, then calf raise in sync with the swing

good_form: The forehand starts well before the swing; rotation of the body drives it, not just the arm.
Use the body as a kinetic chain: hips and upper back rotate in sequence.
Load the hips back toward the edge of their range, then rotate through to the comfortable, strong middle position.
Think of a slingshot: the lower half loads and then sends the upper half around, so the upper half keeps going after the hips return to the middle.
Separation: load the lower half, then let the upper half rotate a bit further.
Rotate against the strong normal toe position and come back to it; push against the ground and turn the back to load the hips.
Choose whichever stance (open, semi-open, neutral, closed) lets you stay balanced and rotate for that ball, rather than fixating on the stance name.
On a fast, deep ball, load the hips and use the slingshot to throw the arm at the target.
When stepping forward, turn the toe out so you can rotate into the ball.
Stay balanced to keep the racket face angle steady and the forehand consistent.
Make contact near the beginning or middle of the arm's range, where the arm is strongest, like the strong part of a push-up.
Turn the chest while keeping the arm's range, so the racket has plenty of room to speed up and then slow down after contact.
Step into the ball so the body can release energy forward; more load means more power released.
With legs and shoulders set correctly and the arm in its range, the arm works almost on autopilot.

faults.name: Over-focusing on the swing
faults.looks_like: Trying to fix forehand problems only through the arm swing rather than the body setup before it.
faults.why_it_matters: The forehand starts before the swing, so fixing only the swing leaves the real issues unsolved.
causes: Thinking about the swing too much
fixes: Work on rotation, footwork, and arm range first
outcome_effects: Inconsistent forehands

faults.name: Rotating to the end of the hip range
faults.looks_like: Stepping into the ball and rotating to the edge of the hip range, with toes and center moving past the strong normal position.
faults.why_it_matters: It feels uncomfortable and forces you to stop or slow down to rotate.
causes: Stance or toe direction that doesn't match the middle of the range when stepping in
fixes: Rotate against the normal position and return to it
Turn the toe out when stepping forward so you can rotate into the ball
Hit the ball with the stance that matches your range
outcome_effects: Rotation slows down
Loss of power from the slingshot

faults.name: Stance that blocks rotation
faults.looks_like: Stepping so the hips can't wind up and rotate toward the racket, e.g. stepping the wrong way on a fast, deep ball.
faults.why_it_matters: Without rotation you have to use just the arm, and balance is lost.
causes: Choosing a stance for the ball's position instead of for balance and rotation
Poor footwork to the ball
fixes: Pick the stance that allows you to load the hips and rotate
On a fast deep ball, use an open or semi-open stance to load the hips
Turn the toe out when stepping forward
outcome_effects: Arm-only swing
Lost balance
Changed racket face angle
Inconsistent forehands

faults.name: Contact at the end of the arm's range
faults.looks_like: Making contact with the arm at the far end of its range, or swinging the arm with no range, then finishing to turn the body.
faults.why_it_matters: The arm pulls the body forward instead of the slingshot effect, so you feel tight and muscle the ball with no room to speed up.
causes: Not turning the chest while keeping the arm's range
Arm already stretched or stuck near the body so no range remains
fixes: Make contact nearer the beginning or middle of the arm's range
Turn the chest/hips while keeping the arm in place so the racket has more range to travel
Practice with an oncoming ball or machine
outcome_effects: Tight, muscled swing
Slow racket head speed
Unable to realize true racket head speed from rotation

good_form: Take the racquet all the way back behind you before starting the shot, while keeping the swing compact.
Get the racquet back with a body turn. The whole body turns, not just the arm.
Generate power from the full body turn into contact.
Keep the racquet face pointing at the target at contact for as long as possible, because its direction decides where the ball goes.
Through the swing, contact and finish, the palm and the racquet face point away from the body. The face never turns toward the body.
Finish with a smooth, continuous motion all the way over the shoulder, like a golf swing finish.
Never stop the racquet during the swing.
Fight the natural urge to tense at contact. Let go, and let the racquet and the rotation do the work.

faults.name: Racquet face turns toward the body
faults.looks_like: The racquet face or palm side faces the body during the swing, at contact or in the follow-through, instead of pointing away.
faults.why_it_matters: It stops you from releasing into the shot and spoils the racquet path into contact and the direction of the hit.
fixes: Keep the palm and racquet face pointing away from the body through the swing, contact and finish.
outcome_effects: Wrong racquet path into contact and poor direction of the ball.

faults.name: Short or rushed finish
faults.looks_like: The swing finishes short next to the body, or too quickly, with a jerky motion and no full follow-through.
faults.why_it_matters: The shot feels too compact and it is hard to let go into it.
causes: Not finishing all the way through the shot.
Finishing too quickly.
fixes: Make the motion smooth and continuous, finishing over the shoulder like a golf swing.
Do not stop the racquet at any point.
outcome_effects: The shot loses power and accuracy.

faults.name: Tensing at contact
faults.looks_like: The body tightens up as the racquet meets the ball.
faults.why_it_matters: Tensing stops you from releasing and letting the racquet and rotation do the work.
causes: It is the body's natural response to tense at contact.
fixes: Fight the urge to tense.
Let go and release, and allow the racquet and the rotation to do the work.
outcome_effects: The shot is less powerful and less accurate.

faults.name: Racquet not taken back far enough or swing too big
faults.looks_like: The racquet does not go all the way back behind the body, or the swing is so big that contact becomes hard.
faults.why_it_matters: A good backswing prepares the shot and supplies the power. The further back the racquet goes, the harder it is to make contact, so the swing has to stay compact.
causes: Taking the racquet back with the arm only, with no body turn.
fixes: Turn the whole body to take the racquet back.
Keep the swing compact but still going all the way back.
outcome_effects: Less power from the body turn.
